issues.title: Digest/frontier convergence for checkpoint-less state recovery (residuals from #238)
issues.body:
## Context

The #238 fix (PR: rehydration wedge / zombie subscription / policy misreport) introduced `StateServed` convergence evidence: bootstrap requesters keep asking until a holder actually serves them, with exact checkpoint-HWM gating where owner checkpoints exist. Three residuals were consciously accepted and documented in-code because closing them requires protocol work beyond a recovery hotfix:

1. **Cross-topic loss window for checkpoint-less state.** The full-state response travels on the main topic and its `StateServed` marker on the `/state-sync` side topic, with no cross-topic ordering/delivery coupling. If the full delta is lost while the marker survives AND the replica is already non-empty (e.g. from one live incremental delta), the requester stops with incomplete history. The marker also latches "a holder served *someone*", not "served *us*" (a double-delivery-loss race). Checkpoint-bearing KV stores are immune (the HWM gate only passes by merging the delta that carried the checkpoint); task lists and never-checkpointed stores are the exposure.
2. **Deletion cold-sync for checkpoint-less deltas.** `full_delta()` carries only live entries — no OR-Set tombstones — so a full response cannot delete a stale replica's obsolete keys unless it carries an owner checkpoint (checkpoint adoption is a verified full replace, and the #238 PR made empty checkpointed owners serve exactly that). issues.title: v0.33.0: CRDT-subscription rehydration wedges when a joined store's owner is offline — daemon's OWN stores never surface
issues.body:
Found while building the x0x-symphony tracker-integrity-v2 two-daemon harness (x0x-symphony#10 / PR #11), reproduced on the v0.33.0 tag build (macOS arm64, loopback pair, `--no-hard-coded-bootstrap`, per-daemon `identity_dir`).

## Repro
1. Daemon A and B, mutually bootstrapped; A creates its own store `aown` (append_only) and writes a key; A also JOINS B's store `bown` (`POST /stores/bown/join` with expected_owner).
2. SIGKILL both daemons.
3. Restart **A only** (B stays down).
4. `GET /stores` on A stays EMPTY for 30s+ — including A's OWN `aown` store; keys are unreadable through the topic routes.

Log shows `loaded 2 persisted CRDT subscriptions from .../crdt-subscriptions.json` but the `CRDT subscription rehydration complete` line never appears — rehydration appears to block/fail on the joined store whose owner is unreachable, and the daemon's own stores are held hostage behind it.

## Control cases (same build)
- Own store only (no joined stores): restart → listed and readable at t+0s, `rehydration complete restored=1`.
- Joined store whose owner IS up at restart: rehydration completes, missed deltas catch up ~15s.

## Expected
Rehydration of owned stores must not depend on the reachability of unrelated joined stores' owners; a joined store with an offline owner should rehydrate in a degraded/pending state (or be skipped with telemetry), not wedge the loop.

issues.title: Replicated tracker integrity: signed state transitions + atomic convergent consumption
issues.body:
## Context

Found during the adversarial review of PR #9 (issue #6 fix). The approval-consumption mechanism (`ApprovalConsumed`, `ApprovalBlob`, gate-side consumption in `approval_gate_decision`) predates PR #9 — it was introduced in d7c26e3 (core types) and 697d166 (consent-gated dispatch), shipped since v0.1.0. PR #9 reuses it and adds cryptographic signing/verification of consumption records, but the underlying storage update is still a non-atomic read-modify-write.

## Finding (Critical, deferred by design from PR #9)

`crates/x0x-symphony-tracker-x0x-crdt/src/lib.rs` — `store_approval` / `store_consumed` both do:

1. `approval_blob_for_issue(issue_id)` (read the whole `ApprovalBlob` from the symphony KvStore)
2. push the new event/consumption onto the in-memory vec
3. `put_approval_blob` (write the whole blob back)

Consequences under concurrency:

- **Both-nodes-consume race**: two orchestrators on different nodes (or a partition reunion) can each evaluate the same valid approval, each mint a consumption record, and each dispatch — the approval is spent twice. - **Overwrite-erases-consumption**: a concurrent `store_approval` (operator approves again) racing a `store_consumed` (gate dispatches) can clobber the other writer's update — the blob written last wins, silently dropping either the new approval event or the consumption record. Dro

issues.title: Audit: cap all peer-drivable buffers/queues (memory-exhaustion class — quic-go/quiche/LSQUIC/msquic CVE parallels)
issues.body:
## Summary

Read-only audit for the **peer-drivable buffer / queue memory-exhaustion class**: *any peer-drivable buffer or queue without a hard cap becomes a remote memory-exhaustion DoS.* This class produced real CVEs across every major QUIC stack:

- **quic-go CVE-2023-49295** (GHSA-ppxx-5m9h-6vxf): PATH_CHALLENGE flood → unbounded queued PATH_RESPONSE, drained slower than filled via congestion/RTT manipulation.
- **quic-go CVE-2024-22189** (GHSA-c33x-xqrf-c478): NEW_CONNECTION_ID + Retire Prior To flood → unbounded queued RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID.
- **Cloudflare quiche CVE-2024-1765** (GHSA-78wx-jg4j-5j6g): unlimited post-handshake 1-RTT CRYPTO frames → unbounded CRYPTO buffering.
- **LSQUIC CVE-2025-54939 "QUIC-LEAK"**: coalesced Initial datagrams; trailing RFC-violating packets allocated but never freed, pre-handshake (before connection-level limits apply).
- **msquic CVE-2024-26190** (GHSA-2x7m-gf85-3745): repeated transport-parameter decode leak during handshake.

**Headline result: ant-quic is NOT exposed to any of these. All five scope items are bounded.** The quinn-lineage core retains upstream's caps, and the bespoke NAT-traversal code adds its own per-session limits, rate limits, and periodic cleanup. Two latent hardening items (both **not currently remotely reachable**) are noted at the end.

Cross-references: #210 (failed-session connection-state retention, fixed in #211) and #214 (assembler out-of-order gap cap). This audit does not overlap their fixes.

issues.title: flake: cancel_before_rename_leaves_memory_clean_and_retry_writes — cancelled tokio::fs write leaves .tmp debris under load
issues.body:
## Symptom

`server::crdt_subscriptions::tests::cancel_before_rename_leaves_memory_clean_and_retry_writes` fails intermittently under full-suite parallel load (observed 4× on 2026-07-14 on an M-series Mac, both on main-derived branches and never in isolation — 25/25 single-test runs pass, module-only runs ~1/10):

```
panicked at src/server/crdt_subscriptions.rs:1194:9:
assertion `left == right` failed: cancelled write left temp-file debris
  left: 1
 right: 0
```

## Mechanism (suspected)

The test drives `persist_recorded` to its first disk await and drops it (cancellation-before-rename window), then asserts no `.tmp` debris. But dropping the future cannot cancel the already-dispatched blocking `tokio::fs` operation: the temp-file **create** runs on the blocking pool and can complete *after* the TempFile guard's Drop cleanup has already run. Under CPU contention (full nextest suite, ~14 concurrent test processes) the blocking pool lags enough for the create to land late → orphaned `.tmp` → assertion fails.

This is mostly a test-expectation race, but it also documents a small real hygiene gap: a cancelled registration write can leak one `.tmp` file that nothing sweeps.

## Notes

- nextest runs each test in its own process, so this is machine-load-sensitive, not cross-test state.
- The same loaded runs also reproduced the #228 reconnect-family flakes (`transport_disconnect_is_reconnect_eligible_and_recovers` failed in the same capture) — different root cause, listed for cor

issues.title: Port quinn fed0321a: error on too many gaps in assembler (reassembly-buffer memory hardening)
issues.body:
## Summary

Upstream quinn landed a reassembly-buffer hardening fix on 2026-06-18 that ant-quic does not have: quinn-rs/quinn@fed0321a *"proto: yield error on too many gaps in assembler"*. Without it, a peer sending maliciously small/gapped STREAM (or CRYPTO) frames can force the assembler to buffer an unbounded number of chunk entries, growing memory per connection. ngtcp2 guards the same vector with a threshold of 4000 chunks; quinn chose a more conservative 1024.

ant-quic's `src/connection/assembler.rs` shares the quinn assembler structure (`insert` + over-allocation-triggered `defragment`) but has no cap on chunk count after defragmentation, so the port is direct.

## Upstream change (quinn fed0321a)

- `Assembler::insert(...)` now returns `Result<(), TooManyChunks>`.
- After a defragmentation pass is triggered by the existing over-allocation threshold, if `self.data.len() > 1024` still holds, return `Err(TooManyChunks)` — i.e. the data is genuinely gapped into >1024 chunks that defrag cannot merge, which only happens under pathological/malicious sending patterns.
- Callers convert the error into a connection-fatal `TransportError::INTERNAL_ERROR`:
  - `connection/mod.rs`: crypto stream insert → `"too many gaps in crypto stream buffer"`.
  - `connection/streams/recv.rs`: stream data insert (skipped when the stream is already stopped) → `"too many gaps in stream buffer"`.

## Why it matters for ant-quic

- Memory-exhaustion hardening in the same family as #210: per-connec

#### Summary

Two daemons using ant-quic's `Node` API on the same host but on different logical planes (e.g., prod UDP 5483 + testnet UDP 6483) discover each other via first-party mDNS and auto-connect, because:

issues.title: pubsub: anchor nodes saturate under fanout burst — shard topics write-lock, fix stage attribution, audit remaining global mutexes (from x0x#186)
issues.body:
## Summary

Investigation of saorsa-labs/x0x#186 (anchor node's gossip dispatcher backs up under fanout burst: `dispatcher_timed_out=25`, `recv_depth` 5 815/10 000) root-caused the saturation to pubsub handler serialization in this crate. Under a 200 msg × 4096 B fanout burst on a 6-node testnet, the anchor node (receiving ~1.73× a leaf's traffic, 383 K msgs vs 220 K) spent **97.2 %** of handler wall-time in two stages:

| Stage | share of handler time | max single |
|---|---|---|
| `dedupe_lock_acquire` | **49.6 %** (9 355 s / 18 853 s) | 326 ms |
| `republish` | **47.6 %** | 29 310 ms |

Notably `drop_full=0` everywhere (no data loss; the priority-shed path never engaged) and `per_peer_timeout=0` on the anchor (per-peer sends fine). All x0x nodes run the worker pool at its 32 ceiling. Data: x0x soak `soak-baseline-20260706T210414`, `diagnostics/fanout_burst/`.

## Root cause

1. **Single topics write-lock.** Every message's dedupe/cache path serializes 32 workers on one `self.topics.write().await` (`crates/pubsub/src/lib.rs:4967`) — a global `RwLock` over all topics.
2. **Republish stage timing is probably mis-attributed.** The dispatcher forward path sends with `detach_accounting = true` (`lib.rs:5118`), so the 47.6 % republish time cannot be slow-peer waiting; it is likely the same lock contention (or task-scheduling latency) charged to the wrong stage. The stage instrumentation needs correcting before the next measurement is trusted.

issues.title: tailnet: cryptographic agent attestation in forward header (eliminates unannounced-agent window, completes #192)
issues.body:
## Context

PR #201 fixed the agent_id inference bug on the inbound forward ACL (#192) by resolving ALL agents on the transport-authenticated machine from the discovery cache and checking the ACL for every one (fail-closed for multi-agent machines).

## Residual window

The agent set comes from the identity **discovery cache**, populated from machine-signed IdentityAnnouncements propagated via gossip. An agent that has started but whose announcement has not yet propagated is absent from the cache and therefore not checked. A hostile agent starting on a machine could receive an inbound forward before its announcement reaches the peer.

## Proposed fix

Require a signed agent attestation in the forward header (ML-DSA-65 signature from the agent key), verified against the agent public key. This requires:

1. Extending DiscoveredAgent to store agent_public_key (populated from the v2 gossip envelope that already carries it).
2. A forward-header wire-format change (ForwardV2): carry opener_agent_id + ML-DSA-65 signature over the header bytes.
3. The inbound side verifies the signature against the cached agent public key, confirms the agent is on the authenticated machine, then runs the ACL check for that specific authenticated agent.

This eliminates both the multi-agent ambiguity AND the unannounced-agent window: the opener proves its identity cryptographically, independent of whether its announcement has propagated.

See PR #201 design note Option 1 for details.

Refs #192, #201.

issues.title: [security] PeerRelay: enforce require_contact_to_relay and add rate/bandwidth limits before real-world opt-in
issues.body:
From the 2026-07-07 production security review of PeerRelay (#177). Two MEDIUMs — both gated behind the code-enforced default-off, so nothing is exposed today, but they should land before anyone is told to enable it.

## 1. Open relay when enabled — require_contact_to_relay is stored but never enforced
`disposition_for` (`src/peer_relay.rs:575-618`) authenticates only the RelayHeader signature — which any stranger can produce with a self-generated ML-DSA-65 keypair (`verify()` at `:158-185` checks only that sender_agent_id derives from the embedded self-supplied pubkey). There is no check on who the relaying peer is. `require_contact_to_relay` exists in config but is explicitly not enforced (`src/network.rs:283-291`, `src/peer_relay.rs:242-246`).

**Scenario:** operator sets `[peer_relay] enabled = true`; any peer that can reach the node signs a fresh header and gets DMs forwarded to any dst in the node's discovery cache, spending the relay's uplink.

## 2. No resource limits on the forward path
Neither `peer_relay.rs` nor `spawn_relay_dm_listener` (`src/lib.rs:9954-10077`) imposes max-concurrent-relayed-streams, per-sender rate limits, or bandwidth caps — the only backpressure is the inbound `mpsc::channel(256)`. Contrast with exec, which has per-agent + total concurrency caps.

## Also (LOW, doc drift)

issues.title: [security] Tailnet inbound forward ACL: agent_id is inferred, not authenticated — authorization collapses to machine granularity
issues.body:
From the 2026-07-07 production security review of tailnet Phase 1 (#132/#183). MEDIUM.

The connect ACL is keyed on the exact `(agent_id, machine_id)` pair, but on the inbound path only the `machine_id` is cryptographically authenticated (QUIC peer identity). The `agent_id` is inferred by taking the **first** discovery-cache entry whose machine matches:

- `src/lib.rs:8107-8113` — accept loop resolves the stream's agent via `find(|a| a.machine_id == machine_id)` (arbitrary iteration order)
- consumed at `src/forward.rs:311` `stream.agent()` → `decide_inbound` → `evaluate_connect_gate`
- the outbound opener writes only a protocol byte, never its agent id (`src/streams.rs:207-209` documents "resolved from the machine ... on the inbound path")

**Failure scenario:** machine M hosts agents A (listed in the ACL for `127.0.0.1:22`) and B (not listed). B opens a ForwardV1 stream from M; the accept loop attributes it to whichever agent `find()` returns first — if A, B's stream is authorized to reach SSH. Conversely a listed agent can be spuriously denied. The ACL's agent-level granularity is not enforced; the real authorization boundary is the machine.

Impact is bounded: machines are hardware-pinned, the peer must already be verified + trusted + machine-listed, and the common deployment is one agent per machine. But the ACL model over-promises.

**Options:**
1. Authenticate the opener's agent identity in the forward header (signed by the agent key), or
2. Document that inbound forwa

From the 2026-07-07 production security review of the v0.28/v0.29 key-lifecycle surface (#130, #179/#182). All findings verified against source on main @ 0d28fbb. No CRITICAL/HIGH — revocation is correctly ordered and fail-closed on every live path — but the lifecycle has these MEDIUM gaps:

issues.title: Worker threads panic on Windows when x0xd starts within 5 min of boot: `overflow when subtracting duration from instant` - call sites in saorsa-gossip-membership and ant-quic
issues.body:
## Summary

`x0xd` 0.29.0 tokio worker threads panic with `overflow when subtracting duration from instant` (std `time.rs:445`, the `Sub<Duration> for Instant` impl) when the daemon starts shortly after Windows boots Ã¢â‚¬â€^] the standard auto-start-service configuration. We traced the reachable call sites; the near-deterministic culprit is a 5-minute cutoff computed in saorsa-gossip-membership's maintenance loop.

The same bug class simultaneously **aborted** an `ant-node` 0.14.2 on the same host (its transport fork carries identical code) Ã¢â‚¬â€^] companion issue: https://github.com/WithAutonomi/ant-node/issues/167.

## Mechanism

On Windows, `std::time::Instant` is `QueryPerformanceCounter` with **epoch = boot**. Any `Instant::now() - duration` panics while `duration > time_since_boot`:

```rust
// rustc 31fca3adb, library/std/src/time.rs:441-445
impl Sub<Duration> for Instant {
    fn sub(self, other: Duration) -> Instant {
        self.checked_sub(other).expect("overflow when subtracting duration from instant")
```

A service started 15Ã¢â‚¬â€œ20 s after boot therefore panics on every cutoff window longer than its uptime. macOS (`mach_absolute_time`) has the same near-zero epoch; Linux boots rarely start services this fast, which is why CI never sees it.

## Observed failure

| | |
|---|---|
| Host | Windows 10 Pro N for Workstations 19045 |
| Binary | `x0xd 0.29.0` (release download), auto-start Windows service (WinSW), SYSTEM |
| Boot | 2026-07-06 17:25:11 UTC |
| x0

issues.title: Config footgun: prod, testnet, and :443 daemons all read the same default connect-ACL path
issues.body:
## Summary

On the VPS bootstrap hosts, the co-located daemons (`x0xd.service`, `x0xd-testnet.service`, and the ADR-0011 `:443` root) all resolve the connect ACL from the **same default path** `/etc/x0x/connect-acl.toml`, because none of them pass `--connect-acl`. Creating that file to configure one plane latently arms **all** of them on their next restart / self-upgrade.

## Evidence (v0.29.0 soak, 2026-07-07)

```
prod   ExecStart=/opt/x0x/x0xd          --config /etc/x0x/config.toml
test   ExecStart=/opt/x0x/x0xd-testnet  --name testnet --no-hard-coded-bootstrap --config /etc/x0x/config-testnet.toml
```

Neither passes `--connect-acl`, so both fall back to the default `/etc/x0x/connect-acl.toml`. To run the tailnet forward soak on **testnet only**, I had to isolate the ACL to `/etc/x0x/connect-acl-testnet.toml` via a systemd drop-in (`--connect-acl <testnet-path>`) so a testnet policy could never leak into prod on a prod restart.

- The connect ACL is a **security policy** (default-deny per-flow connectivity). Two planes silently sharing one policy file is a latent way for a test/dev policy to activate on prod.
- It's non-obvious: the daemons look isolated (separate binaries, configs, data dirs, ports) but converge on one security file.

## Asks

1. Give each network plane its own connect-ACL path by default — either derive it from `--name` / the config, or point the deploy's testnet unit at a plane-specific `--connect-acl` path out of the box.
2. Optiona

issues.title: [revocation] Bring gossip EP3 (dm_inbox) to machine-id revocation parity with the direct path
issues.body:
Flagged by the #177 and #182 security reviews.

**Gap:** the gossip DM revocation gate (EP3, src/dm_inbox.rs ~286-291) checks **agent-id revocation only**, with an explicit `// Intentional for now — machine-id revocation for the DM path is tracked as a follow-up` note. The raw-QUIC **direct** DM path (PR #182, #179) and EP1/EP2 check **both agent AND machine** revocation.

**Consequence:** a peer whose MACHINE is revoked (but whose agent-id isn't separately revoked) can still deliver DMs via the gossip path, while the direct path now drops them. Asymmetry.

**Ask:** update EP3 to also call `is_machine_revoked(machine_id)` (mirroring `direct::inbound_peer_revoked`), so both DM paths are consistently fail-closed on machine revocation. Small change; add a test that a machine-revoked (agent-clean) sender's gossip DM is dropped.

Relates to #130 (key lifecycle enforcement), #179, #182. Low-medium priority — a completeness gap, not an active bypass in the common case.

issues.title: [test] End-to-end byte-stream (open_bi/accept_bi) over a MASQUE-relayed connection
issues.body:
Follow-up from the PR #201 audit (v0.27.28).

All node_app_streams tests use DIRECT loopback connections. The design doc argues app/internal stream separation holds over relayed connections 'by construction' (the reader task owns accept_bi for direct AND relayed connections), and that reasoning is sound — but it is UNTESTED for the MASQUE relay path.

**Why it matters now:** the downstream project x0x just landed PeerRelay (#158) and is building Tailscale-style port-forwarding on open_bi/accept_bi (tailnet #132). Its T7 e2e proof must exercise a forwarded connection over a relayed peer connection. x0x should NOT ship relay-dependent forwarding until an ant-quic-level relayed byte-stream test exists.

**Ask:** add an e2e test that opens a bidi app byte-stream between two peers connected via MASQUE relay (not direct), echoes data both directions, and asserts integrity + that accept_bi yields the app stream (not internal relay framing). The design doc noted 'infrastructure not present' — wire it up or document the relay-test harness gap explicitly.

issues.title: [test] Add drain-on-shutdown regression test for Node::accept_bi
issues.body:
Follow-up from the PR #201 audit (v0.27.28).

The accept_bi drain fix (biased select so queued app-stream handles are drained before the ShuttingDown arm fires) is correct in code (`p2p_endpoint.rs` accept_bi, `biased;` + rx.recv() first) but has NO dedicated regression test. Blocker 1 (the read_exact DoS timeout) got its test (the starved-prefix case ~p2p_endpoint.rs:12550); this one didn't.

**Ask:** add a test that queues ≥1 app-stream handle into app_bi_tx, triggers shutdown, and asserts accept_bi returns the queued handle(s) BEFORE returning ShuttingDown (i.e. the queue is drained, not abandoned). This guards against a future refactor dropping the `biased;` keyword and silently reintroducing the shutdown-vs-recv race that would drop in-flight forwarded streams. Low effort.

issues.title: [investigation] Does the raw-QUIC direct DM path enforce revocation per-message like the gossip path (#130 EP3)?
issues.body:
**Surfaced by the PeerRelay security review (#177), 2026-07-05.**

## Finding
The #130 revocation enforcement (v0.28.0) added EP3 — a per-message `is_agent_revoked` drop in `src/dm_inbox.rs:545` (the gossip DM inbox path). ## Question
Is a **revoked peer on an already-established direct QUIC connection** actually stopped from delivering DMs? - If there's a real gap, a revoked peer that keeps a live direct connection open could keep sending DMs (and, pre-#177, via relay too — now closed for the relay path).
- The tailnet sprint (#132) builds byte-streams on the direct/verified path — the T1 verified gate must genuinely refuse revoked/expired peers.

issues.title: feat(exec-acl): add deny_unknown_fields to exec ACL structs
issues.body:
## Background

The connect ACL (`src/connect/acl.rs`, ADR-0019) deliberately applies `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` to the `[connect]` section and `[[connect.allow]]` entries. This means a misspelled key (`taregts`, `enable`) fails loudly at load time rather than silently yielding a different (potentially more permissive) policy.

The exec ACL (`src/exec/acl.rs`) does not yet have this treatment. A misspelled exec ACL key currently silently disables exec (the safer side of fail-closed — worse than the connect case), but the behavior is inconsistent and can mask operator mistakes.

## Work

Apply `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` to the exec ACL TOML structs, mirroring the connect ACL:

- `ExecSectionToml` (the `[exec]` section struct)
- `ExecAllowEntryToml` (the `[[exec.allow]]` entry struct)
- `ExecAllowCommandToml` (the `[[exec.allow.commands]]` entry struct, if applicable)

Note: do **not** apply to the root file envelope (so other top-level sections can coexist in a future unified config — same reasoning as connect ACL).

## Acceptance

- A misspelled key (`taregts = []`, `enable = true` instead of `enabled = true`) in an exec ACL TOML fails with a clear parse error.
- `x0xd --check --exec-acl <file-with-typo>` exits non-zero.
- Existing exec ACL unit tests (`tests/exec_acl_unit.rs`) continue to pass.
- Update exec ACL documentation (`docs/exec.md`) to mention the unknown-field behavior.

## Related

- ADR-0019 (`docs/adr/0019-connect-acl-default-closed.md`) — documents th

issues.title: task-list REST handlers must consult MLS group membership for group-scoped topics
issues.body:
## Context

[x0x-symphony XSY-0021](https://github.com/saorsa-labs/x0x-symphony) (MLS-encrypted task-list dispatch) depends on x0xd enforcing MLS group isolation on task-list REST endpoints.

## Current behavior

The `/task-lists/:id/tasks` handlers in `src/server/mod.rs` (routes at lines 2275-2279) are plain topic-keyed routes. They do **not** consult `named_groups` or `mls_groups` membership. Task lists are keyed by arbitrary topic string and appear unencrypted unless a caller uses the separate `crdt/encrypted.rs` layer (which is not wired into REST task-list sync).

## Required

For symphony's MLS dispatch (XSY-0021) to provide **enforced** group isolation (not just scoped/best-effort), the task-list REST handlers must:

1. Recognize group-scoped task-list IDs (symphony uses the convention `x0x.group.<group_id>.symphony.<list_id>`).
2. Consult the named-group / MLS membership for the requesting agent.
3. Return `403 Forbidden` (or empty) for non-members attempting to read/write group-scoped task lists.

## Impact

Without this, symphony's MLS dispatch is scoped/best-effort: workers outside the group can still read group-scoped task-list topics if they know the ID. The two-daemon isolation test in XSY-0021 is `#[ignore]` because it cannot prove hard isolation against the current REST behavior.

## Related

- x0x-symphony XSY-0021: MLS-encrypted task-list dispatch
- x0x-symphony `v0.0.M3` tag annotation discloses this as a best-effort boundary

issues.title: [test/WS1.1] deferred stalled-reader integration harness for per-WS outbound-queue slow-consumer close
issues.body:
## Context

Follow-up to PR #147 (WS1.1 / #122), which bounded the per-WebSocket outbound queue to `WS_OUTBOUND_CAPACITY=1024` with a slow-consumer close (WS 1013). The PR shipped **11 deterministic unit tests** (9 feeder-policy + 2 extracted-writer slow-close) as the CI gate but explicitly deferred a dedicated stalled-reader integration harness.

## What the deferred test would prove

An end-to-end assertion that a stalled local WS reader — one that accepts the socket but stops draining frames — causes:

1. the per-session outbound mpsc queue to fill (`ws_outbound_dropped` to climb for topic frames), and
2. the session to be closed with a **1013 Try Again Later** close code within a bounded wall-clock window (the keepalive pinger is the reliable detector at a 30s cadence), incrementing `ws_slow_consumer_closes`.

This is the real-world failure mode the design defends against: a misbehaving local client cannot grow daemon memory without bound.

## Why it was deferred (the documented obstacle)

A literal OS/TCP stalled-reader harness was found **not viable** with the current topology. The multi-layer buffering pipeline — `gossip → broadcast(256) → outbound(1024) → writer → TCP send buffer` — prevents the per-session mpsc queue from filling via any *external* frame flood:

issues.title: [feature] POST /agent/sign — sign payloads with the daemon agent key (unblocks x0x-symphony XSY-0020)
issues.body:
## Rationale

x0x-symphony signs claims/handoffs with the agent's ML-DSA-65 key, but it consumes x0xd over REST only (no Rust linkage) and must never touch key material. The stateless verification counterpart \`POST /agent/verify\` already shipped in v0.23.1 (PR #109); this adds the signing half so external consumers can produce signatures the fleet can verify.

Cross-repo blocker: x0x-symphony XSY-0020 ("x0x:agent-sign-endpoint").

## Design

\`POST /agent/sign\` → \`{ context: string, payload: base64 }\` → \`{ agent_id, signature: base64, context }\`. Follow the \`/agent/verify\` handler + endpoint-registry pattern (\`src/api/mod.rs\`), CLI \`x0x agent sign\`.

## Security constraints (must-have)

- Loopback + bearer-token API only (standard auth middleware; NOT auth-exempt).
- **Domain separation is mandatory**: the daemon signs \`DST(context) || payload\`, where \`context\` is a required non-empty ASCII string (e.g. \`"x0x-symphony-handoff-v1"\`) and the DST encoding is length-prefixed so no \`(context, payload)\` pair can collide with another — and, critically, the DST namespace must be provably disjoint from every internal x0x signing input (announcements, group commits, certificates, upgrade manifests). Reserve a prefix byte/namespace for external signing so a caller can never trick the daemon into signing a valid protocol message. Enumerate current internal signing input formats in the PR to prove disjointness.
- Reject a denylist of internal context strings; require

issues.title: [epic] Tailnet Phase 1 remaining scope: SOCKS5 and real-NAT/relay acceptance
issues.body:
## Goal

Let a user connect their own machines over any network (home NAT, CGNAT, hotel wifi, LTE) with \`ssh -L\`-style ergonomics: a local TCP listener on machine A tunnels to a service on machine B over x0x's PQC QUIC transport — no TUN, no kernel extensions, works on every OS.

## Why now (2026-07-02 gap analysis)

ant-quic already carries the two hardest Tailscale pieces:
- native QUIC NAT traversal (no STUN/ICE/TURN), and
- an **always-on symmetric MASQUE relay fallback** (\`ant-quic/src/masque/\`, \`enable_relay_fallback: true\` at \`nat_traversal_api.rs:625-626\`; every node relays — no DERP fleet to operate).

The gap is above the wire: x0x today speaks only message-level \`Node::send\`/\`recv\` (\`network.rs:2313-2360\`). ant-quic's \`high_level::Connection\` exposes \`open_bi()\`/\`accept_bi()\` reliable streams and datagrams (\`high_level/connection.rs:447,632\`) — public, but unused by x0x. Phase 1 is the plumbing + product around those streams. The transport is E2E post-quantum (ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65) — relays forward ciphertext only. This is the wedge WireGuard/Tailscale don't have.

## Deliverables

1. **Per-peer stream API**: expose bidirectional byte streams between verified peers through \`NetworkNode\`/\`Agent\` (open/accept, protocol-id framing so streams coexist with gossip/DM traffic, backpressure-correct copy loops).
2. **Forwarder service in x0xd**: \`forward add <local-port> <peer> <remote-host:port>\` → local TCP listener → peer stream → remote TCP c

issues.title: [prereq] Key lifecycle: expiry, re-auth, and revocation for machine/agent identities
issues.body:
## Context (2026-07-02 Tailscale gap analysis)

Machine/Agent/User keys are long-lived files in \`~/.x0x/\` with no expiry, no re-auth, and no enforced revocation. \`AgentCertificate\` supports revocation conceptually but there is no CRL/expiry enforcement anywhere. ant-quic has cert rotation/expiry machinery (\`crypto/certificate_manager.rs\`) that x0x does not use.

## Why it matters

Fine for gossip identity; **unacceptable for device connectivity** (tailnet Phase 1): a lost or stolen laptop stays reachable/authorized forever. Tailscale's default node-key expiry is 180 days for exactly this reason. This is a hard prerequisite — no data-plane feature (streams, port-forwarding, SOCKS) ships without it.

## Scope

1. **Expiry**: optional \`not_after\` on machine/agent identity records + AgentCertificate; daemon refuses expired peers on the verified path (same gate that feeds \`inbound.verified\`).
2. **Re-auth**: a re-sign flow — user key re-issues the AgentCertificate; CLI \`x0x identity renew\`.
3. **Revocation**: signed revocation record gossiped + persisted (KvStore or dedicated topic); verified-gate checks the revocation set. Design must be partition-tolerant (revocation eventually propagates; cached-peer trust honors it on receipt).
4. Defaults: existing deployments unaffected (no expiry unless set); tailnet enrollment (future) sets expiry by default.

## Acceptance criteria

- Expired or revoked identity fails the verified gate; test proves an exec request and a DM fro

issues.title: [low] Replace dead unreachable!() match arms in src/bin/x0x.rs with explicit errors
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 panic-safety scan)

The only two compile-present panic sites in production code are:
- \`src/bin/x0x.rs:1718\` — \`Commands::Upgrade { .. } => unreachable!()\`
- \`src/bin/x0x.rs:1755\` — \`... | Commands::Autostart { .. } => unreachable!()\` (also covers Routes, Tree, Uninstall, Purge, Constitution, UserId, Start, Instances)

Both are provably dead today: every listed variant is dispatched with an early \`return\` in the same function (~1152–1206), so the second match only sees unhandled variants. But if a future refactor removes one early-return, the arm becomes a live panic — and the panic-scanner precedent (#109: scanner blind spots) says don't rely on dead code staying dead.

## Proposed fix

Replace \`unreachable!()\` with an explicit error return (\`anyhow::bail!("command dispatched earlier — dispatch table out of sync")\` or the CLI's error type), preserving exhaustiveness.

## Acceptance criteria

- Zero \`unreachable!()\` in production code (\`src/\`, bins) — scanner-verifiable.
- CLI behavior unchanged for all commands (existing CLI tests green).
- fmt/clippy/nextest green.

issues.title: [low] Ensure release workflow cannot ship on red CI
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 production-readiness review)

\`.github/workflows/release.yml\` validates release metadata and signs artifacts, but has no test/clippy gate of its own — it appears to rely on \`ci.yml\` having passed on the same commit, without enforcing it. A tag pushed on a commit with red (or still-running, or skipped) CI would still ship.

## Proposed fix (either)

- In release.yml, add a first job that queries the Checks API for the tagged SHA and fails unless the CI workflow concluded \`success\` (\`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{sha}/check-runs\` or \`workflow_run\` trigger gating), **or**
- Run the cheap gates (fmt, clippy -D warnings, nextest) directly in release.yml before build/sign/publish.

## Acceptance criteria

- Demonstrated: a tag on a commit whose CI failed causes release.yml to fail before any artifact is published (test on a scratch tag).
- Documented in docs/cicd.md.

issues.title: [low] Constant-time API token comparison + reduce ?token= query-param exposure
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 security-surface audit)

Two low-severity items in the (otherwise solid) local API auth:

1. \`src/server/mod.rs:2579\` and \`:2592\` compare the bearer token with plain \`==\` — non-constant-time, a theoretical timing side-channel. Loopback-only bind makes this low, not high. The \`subtle\` crate is not currently a dependency.
2. \`accepts_query_token\` (\`src/server/mod.rs:2611-2623\`) allows \`?token=\` for browser endpoints (\`/gui\`, \`/ws*\`, \`/events*\`, \`/presence/events\`, ...). The daemon has no access-log middleware recording query strings (verified), so the risk is client-side only: browser history, Referer, devtools/HAR exports.

## Proposed fix

1. Compare via \`subtle::ConstantTimeEq\` (or double-HMAC comparison) — trivial change.
2. For browser endpoints, exchange the long-lived token for a short-lived per-session token: e.g. \`POST /auth/session\` (bearer-authenticated) → expiring one-time token accepted in the query string; GUI JS does the exchange. Keeps SSE/WS ergonomics without putting the durable secret in URLs.

## Acceptance criteria

- No plain \`==\` on token paths; unit test still proves wrong-token → 401.
- Durable API token never accepted via query string (only short-lived session tokens); GUI + WS/SSE e2e still pass.
- fmt/clippy/nextest green.

issues.title: [low] Register crdt/kv sync background tasks with Agent shutdown
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 production-readiness review)

\`TaskListSync::start\` / \`KvStoreSync::start\` spawn long-lived subscription loops and drop the JoinHandles:
- \`src/crdt/sync.rs:136,162\` (delta-merge listener, state-request responder)
- \`src/kv/sync.rs:95,125\` (same pattern)

They are registered neither in the Agent's \`spawn_tracked\` registry (\`lib.rs:3387\`) nor in the server \`bg_tasks\` vector, so \`Agent::shutdown()\` does not abort them — they only end when the gossip runtime drops the topic sender.

(The retry spawns at \`crdt/sync.rs:201\` / \`kv/sync.rs:168\` iterate a fixed schedule and exit — fine.)

## Why it matters

Per-store/per-list task leak, bounded by store count, and the one class of background task outside the (otherwise thorough, issue-#116-hardened) shutdown path. Risky for embedded \`serve()\` (#110) where the host may start/stop agents repeatedly in one process.

## Proposed fix

Route these spawns through \`spawn_tracked\` (they are Agent-owned), or store handles on the sync structs and abort in their teardown, whichever matches the ownership model.

## Acceptance criteria

- All four spawn sites tracked and aborted on \`Agent::shutdown()\`.
- Test: create store/list, shut agent down, assert the subscription tasks terminate (no lingering tasks; e.g. via tokio task instrumentation or a completion channel).
- fmt/clippy/nextest green.

issues.title: [medium] Decompose src/server/mod.rs (25,334 lines) into submodules
issues.body:

\`src/server/mod.rs\` is 25,334 lines — the entire REST surface, handlers, WS/SSE plumbing, auth, state, and their tests in one file (\`lib.rs\` is 10,222 for comparison). It is the single biggest maintainability/review-risk hotspot in the repo.

## Why it matters

- Reviews of server changes cannot be scoped; every PR touches the same giant file → merge conflicts and reviewer fatigue.

## Acceptance criteria

- \`server/mod.rs\` reduced to module wiring + router assembly (< ~2,000 lines).
- \`git diff\` is moves + \`use\` fixes only; endpoint registry (\`x0x routes\`) output unchanged.
- Full nextest green; fmt/clippy clean; no public API change (verify with \`cargo doc\` diff or semver-checks if available).

Coordinate with #110 (serve() extraction) — do this first or a

issues.title: [medium] Ratchet CI line-coverage floor up from 48%
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 production-readiness review)

\`ci.yml\` gates coverage at \`cargo llvm-cov --fail-under-lines 48\`. A 48% line floor is low for a security/crypto daemon: over half the lines can go untested without failing CI.

## Why it matters

x0x's correctness story leans on the e2e/VPS suites (202 \`#[ignore]\`d tests), so unit CI is the only always-on gate. A low floor lets regressions in rarely-exercised branches (error paths, ACL denials, shutdown ordering) land silently.

## Proposed fix — ratchet, don't jump

1. Measure current actual coverage (likely above the floor).
2. Set the floor to (actual − 1) immediately so it can never regress.
3. Ratchet +3–5 points per release toward a 70% target, prioritizing: exec ACL denial paths, auth middleware, storage/identity error paths, shutdown ordering.
4. Keep \`docs/coverage-exclusions.md\` as the mechanism for justified exclusions.

## Acceptance criteria

- CI floor equals current-actual minus a small buffer (no dead headroom).
- A written ratchet schedule in the repo (plan doc or ci.yml comment).
- First ratchet PR adds tests for at least one of the priority areas above.

issues.title: [medium] Wrap bootstrap dial in a timeout (bootstrap.rs connect_with_retry)
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 production-readiness review)

\`src/bootstrap.rs:85\` — \`node.connect_addr(addr).await\` inside \`connect_with_retry\` is **not** wrapped in \`tokio::time::timeout\`.

Every other call site in \`lib.rs\` (2625, 2687, 2818, 3167, 3299, 6461, 6514) wraps \`connect_addr\`/\`connect_cached_peer\` in \`timeout(dial_timeout/CONNECT_TIMEOUT, ...)\`, which implies \`connect_addr\` has no reliable internal timeout.

## Why it matters

If a bootstrap dial hangs, the retry loop hangs on that attempt — the exponential backoff \`sleep\` only runs *after* a returned error, so one black-holed bootstrap address can stall the whole bootstrap round instead of failing over to the next node.

## Proposed fix

Wrap the dial in the same timeout used by the lib.rs call sites (or a bootstrap-specific constant, e.g. 10s), treating timeout as a retryable error so backoff/rotation proceeds.

## Acceptance criteria

- Bootstrap dial is bounded by an explicit timeout; timeout counts as a failed attempt feeding the existing capped backoff (max_retries=3, backoff cap 5s).
- Test: a dial to a non-routable address (e.g. 10.255.255.1:5483 style blackhole or a mock) fails within the timeout and the loop proceeds to the next attempt/peer.
- fmt/clippy/nextest green.

issues.title: [medium] Bound the per-WebSocket-session outbound queue (unbounded_channel in server/mod.rs)
issues.body:
## Finding (2026-07-02 production-readiness review)

\`src/server/mod.rs:18316\` creates the only unbounded channel in production code: \`mpsc::unbounded_channel::<WsOutbound>()\`, the per-WebSocket-session outbound queue.

Three feeders write into it, two of them remote-influenced:
- keepalive pinger (30s, self-limiting)
- direct-message forwarder (\`subscribe_direct\`, ~18358–18374) — driven by **remote DMs**
- per-topic forwarders (~18542+) draining a bounded \`broadcast::channel(256)\` fed by **remote gossip topic traffic**

The consumer is the writer task (~18344) which \`ws_tx.send().await\`s to the socket. If the local WS client stalls (stops reading), \`outbound_rx\` never drains and the queue grows without bound while a remote peer floods a subscribed topic or sends DMs → unbounded daemon memory.

## Why it matters

Everything upstream is bounded (broadcast 256, gossip recv 10_000) — this is the one spot where remote traffic + a misbehaving local client can grow daemon RSS without limit. The 2026-05-27 receive_window incident showed unbounded buffers are exactly how "high resource use" reports happen.

## Proposed fix

Replace with a bounded \`mpsc::channel\` (e.g. 1024) and a slow-consumer policy:
- \`try_send\` from feeders; on \`Full\`, either drop-with-counter (topic frames) or close the WS session with a "slow consumer" close frame (preferred, matches how browsers handle overload).
- Surface drops/closures in \`/diagnostics\` counters.

issues.title: Surface the already-observed peer address (coarsened) for connected peers — origin-diversity signal, off-mesh and raw-IP-free
issues.body:
## Ask

Surface the peer address the transport **already observes** (`connected_peer_snapshot()` / the same source `add_from_connection()` enriches the bootstrap cache from) as an **opt-in, coarse, masked origin token** on **point-to-point surfaces only**:

```
{ observed_prefix: "203.0.113.0/24" | "2001:db8::/48", direct: bool, cgnat: bool }
```

- Optional fields on the DM-receive WS/SSE event + per-peer `GET /diagnostics/dm`. **Never gossiped, never announced, never on `/peers`.**
- **Default OFF** (`observed_prefix_enabled = true` in the daemon TOML). When off — the default — the fields are entirely absent and wire behavior is byte-identical.
- Masks fixed at /24 (v4) and /48 (v6); `direct=false` marks a relayed observation; `cgnat` from the existing RFC 6598 check. Never a raw IP, no GeoIP, no new deps.

## Why this respects the existing lines

- **ADR-0006** is the shape constraint: this is per-connection data delivered only to the participating peer — discovery surfaces and gossip never see it. That is the categorical difference from anything resembling a location broadcast.
- **trust-and-connectivity.md**'s refusal to convert functional metadata into quasi-geolocation is answered structurally: default-off, coarse-only, point-to-point, operator-opted. Reachability capability stays the public vocabulary; this token exists only between two peers who are already connected and therefore already observe each other's addresses at the socket level.
- No collision with ADR-002

issues.title: Node::shutdown(): make fixed-port UDP socket release fully synchronous (tight-loop same-port rebind)
issues.body:
Follow-up to #196 (v0.27.27), low priority. #196 releases the endpoint UDP socket on shutdown — single stop->restart on the SAME fixed QUIC port works reliably (validated end-to-end from x0x). But a TIGHT zero-gap loop that immediately re-binds the same fixed UDP port fails with 'Address already in use (os error 48)' and does not recover even with ~6s of retry.

Traced: Node::shutdown() -> endpoint.release_socket_for_shutdown() (high_level/endpoint.rs:~447) swaps the fixed-port socket for a throwaway ephemeral one and drops the original, but the OS FD for the fixed port closes only when the endpoint driver drops its LAST reference — shortly AFTER shutdown() returns. A single restart absorbs this via the ~5s wait_idle drain; an instantaneous same-port loop does not.

Ask: make the fixed-port socket FD release synchronous within Node::shutdown() (await the driver's last-reference drop before returning), so an immediate same-fixed-port rebind succeeds with no retry. Repro: bind fixed UDP port -> Node::shutdown().await -> immediately bind same port in a loop.

Impact: low. The real embedder pattern (single stop->restart) already works; x0x documents a brief-retry guidance for tight loops. Filing for completeness.

issues.title: presence: stop_beacons() detaches the beacon task on its 5s timeout instead of aborting it
issues.body: Surfaced via x0x #116 (deterministic shutdown). `PresenceManager::stop_beacons()` (saorsa-gossip-presence 0.5.63 src/lib.rs:607) signals + joins its beacon task with an internal 5s timeout (~line 622), and on timeout returns Err while DROPPING/detaching the beacon JoinHandle rather than aborting it (~line 627). A beacon mid-broadcast (per-send timeout ~15s, ~line 521) can therefore outlive a caller that awaited stop_beacons(). Ask: on the stop timeout, abort() the beacon JoinHandle and await it, so the task is guaranteed stopped before stop_beacons() returns. (x0x calls stop_beacons() correctly in PresenceWrapper::shutdown(); this is the dependency-side guarantee gap.)

issues.title: PresenceManager equivalent: stop_beacons() detaches the beacon task on its 5s timeout instead of aborting it
issues.body: Wrong repo guard: this is for saorsa-gossip-presence, filing here only if ant-quic is the right tracker — please move if not. Surfaced via x0x #116. `PresenceManager::stop_beacons()` (saorsa-gossip-presence 0.5.63 src/lib.rs:607) signals + joins its beacon task with an internal 5s timeout (line ~622) and on timeout returns Err while DROPPING/detaching the JoinHandle rather than aborting it (line ~627). A beacon mid-broadcast (per-send timeout ~15s, line ~521) can therefore outlive a caller's shutdown even though the caller awaited stop_beacons(). Ask: on the stop timeout, abort() the beacon JoinHandle (and await it) so the task is guaranteed stopped before stop_beacons() returns. x0x calls stop_beacons() correctly in PresenceWrapper::shutdown(); this is the dependency-side guarantee gap.

issues.title: ExecService::shutdown() should force-cancel in-flight exec sessions (+ kill child processes)
issues.body: Follow-up from #116 (PR for it). `ExecService::shutdown()` now stops the 3 background loops (inbound / peer-lifecycle / session-idle), but does NOT force-cancel per-request exec handler tasks for an in-flight remote command, nor kill their child processes (the `tokio::spawn` in run_inbound_loop for an `ExecFrame::Request`, src/exec/service.rs). Today such a session completes, hits its duration/idle/lease cap, or is reaped on process exit — so for an in-process embedder doing serve→shutdown→restart, a running remote command can briefly outlive shutdown_and_wait(). Scope: track per-request session task handles (+ child PIDs), abort/kill them on shutdown(), add a test that starts a long-running exec then shuts down and asserts the child is gone. Distinct from background-loop teardown (#116).

issues.title: Node::shutdown() should synchronously release the UDP socket (in-process re-bind)
issues.body:
Surfaced while making x0x embeddable in-process (saorsa-labs/x0x #110, PR #115).

When a host runs `x0x` as a library and calls `serve()` → `shutdown_and_wait()`, the QUIC node is shut down (`Node::shutdown().await`, all connections closed, internal tasks aborted), **but the bound UDP socket is not released within the process** — it frees only on process exit. A probe confirmed the socket stays bound for 30s+ after `Node::shutdown()` returned, blocking an in-process re-bind on the same fixed UDP port.

Impact: an embedder that stops and restarts x0x in the same process cannot re-bind a **fixed** QUIC port; it must use an ephemeral port. The daemon binary is unaffected (process exit frees the socket).

## Ask
`Node::shutdown()` (or a dedicated call) should **synchronously release the endpoint's UDP socket** before returning, so the port is immediately re-bindable in-process.

## Repro sketch
1. `NetworkNode::new()` on `0.0.0.0:PORT` (fixed).
2. `node.shutdown().await`.
3. Immediately attempt to bind a UDP socket on `PORT` → currently fails (address in use) for 30s+.

issues.title: x0x::server: deterministic teardown of Agent-internal + ExecService background tasks (Phase 2b of #110)
issues.body:
Follow-up from #110 (PR #115). The embeddable `x0x::server::serve()` lifecycle landed with a **bounded** teardown: `ServerHandle::shutdown_and_wait()` stops the HTTP/SSE server, the server-owned background tasks, the gossip runtime, and the QUIC `NetworkNode`, and releases the API port.

It does **not** yet deterministically stop:
- Agent-internal listeners spawned in `Agent`: identity listener, network-lifecycle listeners, direct listener, capability-advert service.
- `ExecService` tasks (incl. the unconditional `run_session_idle_loop`).

These currently stop only on process exit. For the daemon this is fine (process exits). For an in-process embedder that starts/stops repeatedly, they leak.

## Scope
- Give `Agent` and `ExecService` real shutdown handles / a cancellation token, and have `Agent::shutdown()` (or the server supervisor) await them.
- Classify background tasks critical vs best-effort and propagate critical-task panics.
- Secondary (also from #110 review): after the 2s grace timeout the supervisor aborts stragglers via `AbortHandle` but does not await them; and `join_network` spawned into `bg_tasks` can race `agent.shutdown()` during teardown.

## Acceptance
After `shutdown_and_wait()` returns, no Agent/ExecService background task is still running (verified by a test that starts/stops in-process and asserts no task survives).

issues.title: Publish x0x transport + identity Internet-Draft (ADR-0017 workstream #1)
issues.body:
## Context

[ADR-0017](docs/adr/0017-x0x-as-agent-transport-layer.md) argues that the agent **transport layer** is the open, un-consolidated slot (per the VentureBeat "what solves transport?" framing), and that standards consolidate around **published specs**, not codebases. x0x has strong running code but no published spec; the competing Pilot Protocol has a (weaker, centralized, classical-crypto) IETF Internet-Draft.

## Goal

Publish an Independent-Submission Internet-Draft for x0x's transport + identity model — PQC-native, self-authenticating (no registry/DNS), QUIC-native NAT traversal — structured to diff directly against `draft-teodor-pilot-protocol-01`.

Skeleton already written: [`docs/design/x0x-transport-protocol-id.md`](docs/design/x0x-transport-protocol-id.md).

## Tasks
- [ ] Decide alignment posture vs Pilot Protocol (align / contribute / differentiate)
- [ ] Wire-format ABNF for AgentCard, AgentCertificate, DM frame
- [ ] Canonical bytes + domain separators for every signed object
- [ ] IANA considerations: media types (`application/x0x-agent-card+json`), ALPN, `x0x://` URI scheme, `/.well-known/` registration
- [ ] Lead with the two differentiators no candidate has: **post-quantum** + **zero-registry self-authenticating identity**
- [ ] Submit `draft-saorsa-x0x-agent-transport-00`

## References
- ADR-0017, `docs/design/x0x-transport-protocol-id.md`
- Comparison: Pilot Protocol (`draft-teodor-pilot-protocol-01`), ANP (`did:wba`), libp2p

issues.title: A2A-over-x0x: streaming, push, artifacts and external interoperability (unary implemented)
issues.body:
## Context

[ADR-0017](docs/adr/0017-x0x-as-agent-transport-layer.md) positions x0x as the **transport layer** beneath application agent protocols (A2A, MCP). The **discovery** half shipped in **v0.24.0** (signed `AgentCard` + `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json` A2A adapter). This issue tracks the deferred **delivery** half: the A2A-over-x0x message binding.

## Goal

issues.title: Add a signature-verify surface as the counterpart to POST /agent/sign
issues.body:
## Summary

`POST /agent/sign` (since v0.20.0) produces detached ML-DSA-65 signatures and is explicitly intended for *"applications that persist signed records to disk or distributed storage where transport-layer gossip signing doesn't survive a read."* Such applications must also **verify** those signatures — when reading records back, and when receiving records relayed by third parties. Today x0x exposes no verification surface, so every consumer must bundle its own FIPS-204 library and re-create x0x's signed-byte framing. Confirmed absent on v0.22.0: `POST /agent/verify` returns 404.

Proposed counterpart:

**`POST /agent/verify`** (primary):

```json
// request
{
  "payload_b64": "<base64 payload bytes>",
  "signature_b64": "<base64 detached ML-DSA-65 signature>",
  "public_key_b64": "<base64 ML-DSA-65 public key>",
  "domain": "optional — same semantics as /agent/sign"
}
// response
{ "ok": true, "valid": true, "algorithm": "x0x.agent-sign.v1.ml-dsa-65" }
```

Behaviour: if `domain` is present, verify over `domain || 0x00 || payload` (mirroring the #90 signing convention shipped in v0.22.0); reject malformed/oversize input with 400; same 256 KiB payload cap as `/agent/sign`. Stateless — verification uses only caller-supplied public material; no key access, no identity state.

**Optionally**, a CLI sibling `x0x agent verify --payload-b64 … --signature-b64 … --public-key-b64 … [--domain …]` for scripts and diagnostics. Since verification is stateless it could be daemonless

issues.title: send vs send_replace: DM capability upgrade lost at startup, breaks cross-NAT DM
issues.body:
**Bug:** `start_dm_inbox` upgrades `DmCapabilities` to gossip-ready via `watch::Sender::send`, which drops the value when there are no receivers. At startup it can run before `start_capability_advert_service` subscribes, so the upgrade is lost. The advert then stays at `pending()` (`gossip_inbox=false`) for the process lifetime, peers cache it as non-gossip-ready, and fall back to raw-QUIC. That fails across NAT.

Surfaced while completing the #100 gossip-inbox path: the owner->joiner Welcome arrives over gossip, but the joiner's ChunkAck goes raw-QUIC and never reaches the NAT'd owner, so the transfer stalls.

**Fix:** `send_replace` instead of `send` (stores unconditionally). One line plus a regression test, against v0.21.4 (`src/lib.rs`). Branch ready if useful: `josh-clsn/x0x:fix-dm-cap-send-replace`. Happy to open a PR.

Thanks for the gossip-inbox work; this finishes it for the cross-NAT case.

Cooling (`is_peer_suppressed`) is **exempt** for `TopicPriority::Critical` at the **admission** layer but **NOT** at the **claim/gate** layer. issues.title: Proposal: optional `domain` field on `POST /agent/sign` for safe domain separation
issues.body:
# Proposal: optional `domain` field on `POST /agent/sign` for safe domain separation

## Summary

Add an optional `domain` string field to the `POST /agent/sign` request. When provided, `x0xd` signs `domain || 0x00 || payload` rather than the raw payload. The response echoes the domain back so a verifier knows the canonical-bytes shape without out-of-band context.

## Motivation

`/agent/sign` (added in v0.19.47) signs arbitrary caller-supplied bytes. This is the right primitive: simple, general, lets callers canonicalize their own structured payloads.

But callers signing different KINDS of structured payloads need to add their own domain-separation prefix to prevent cross-protocol signature replay. For example, within one ecosystem:

- A pairing protocol signs a "register" envelope.
- A revocation protocol signs an "unregister" envelope.

Same agent key, different intent — if the canonical bytes overlap by accident, an attacker can take a signature from one context and replay it in another.

The standard mitigation is a domain prefix: `"my-protocol.v1.register" || 0x00 || payload`. This works when callers know to do it, but:

1. **Easy to forget.** Especially in early integrations.
2. **Easy to get wrong.** Separator byte matters (NUL prevents prefix-extension attacks; missing it allows them). Length-prefixing is even safer. Each codebase re-derives this.
3. **Every ecosystem reinvents it.** The same canonical-bytes helper appears in every project signing multi-purpose payl

## Summary

Add a `local:` topic prefix to `x0xd`'s pub/sub. Topics with this prefix are NOT relayed to remote mesh peers — they are delivered only to subscribers attached to the same `x0xd` instance. All other primitives (`/publish`, `/subscribe`, `/events`, bearer-token auth, verified/trust annotations) work unchanged.

`x0xd` is increasingly used as a local-IPC substrate by multi-process applications running on a single machine — the daemon + apps pattern documented in `docs/local-apps.md`. 1. **Roll your own loopback HTTP server.** The app implements its own server on `127.0.0.1`, reimplementing subscribe/publish/auth. Duplicates work `x0xd` already does well, and the surface is easy to get wrong (CSRF, token rotation, etc.).

3. **Use `/direct/send` for point-to-point.** Works for 1-to-1 but doesn't fan out, and doesn't carry the verified/trust annotations gossip does.

issues.title: UdpTransportAdapter::close() does not tear down the ant-quic connection
issues.body:
## Discovery (from PR #11)

`UdpTransportAdapter::close()` clears its tracked-peer map but does **not** call into ant-quic to close the underlying QUIC connections. After `close()`:

- The node is still reachable on the wire.
- SWIM pings still ack.
- Naive failure-injection in integration tests fails — calling `close()` does not produce an unreachable peer.

PR #11's `swim_promotes_unresponsive_peer_to_suspect_then_dead` had to abort the dispatcher task instead, because `close()` did not make node2 unresponsive.

## Why this matters

1. **Test ergonomics**: integration tests need a clean way to simulate "peer goes away". Aborting dispatcher tasks works but is intrusive and depends on test-only access to the dispatcher.
2. **Graceful shutdown semantics**: a daemon calling `close()` expects to release network resources. Leaving the QUIC connection live leaks state and can extend the peer's tracked-alive window on the other side.
3. **Resource leak under reconnect**: a re-`open()` after `close()` might race against the still-live previous connection.

## Suggested direction

`close()` should:
1. Iterate the tracked-peer map and call `ant_quic::Node::close_peer(peer_id)` (or equivalent) for each.
2. After ant-quic confirms the close, clear the tracked-peer map.
3. Optionally wait for the local socket to drain.

Acceptance:
- A test that calls `close()` on node2 then attempts a ping from node1 reports node2 unreachable within the normal SWIM probe timeout.
- No QUIC connections r

issues.title: Privacy Layer 4: x0xd defaults to silent (warn-only) if RUST_LOG unset
issues.body:
## Why

A user installing x0xd via the published binary today gets the framework's default tracing subscriber, which logs at info — including the per-peer recv/send events (until Layer 3 demotes those). This violates privacy-by-default for **anyone running x0xd outside our fleet** (community operators, downstream apps, individual users).

`RUST_LOG=warn` on our fleet (Layer 1) does not protect them.

## Change

In `src/bin/x0xd.rs` initialization, set the tracing subscriber's default filter to `warn` if no `RUST_LOG` env var is set. Users opt in to verbose logging explicitly.

```rust
// at x0xd startup
let filter = EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
    .unwrap_or_else(|_| EnvFilter::new("warn"));
```

(Current code probably has `EnvFilter::from_default_env()` which falls back to info-level for the framework.)

## Acceptance

- [ ] `x0xd` started without `RUST_LOG` set logs only warn/error
- [ ] `RUST_LOG=info x0xd` restores verbose logging for opt-in debugging

issues.title: Privacy Layer 3: demote per-peer info! events to trace! (defense in depth)
issues.body:
## Why

Companion to [#83 (Layer 2)](https://github.com/saorsa-labs/x0x/issues/83) — defense in depth.

Layer 2 makes warn!/error! lines privacy-safe via salted-hash identifiers. But the hot-path `info!` events in x0x::network are still verbose by default and a real risk if anyone bumps `RUST_LOG` on a prod node for debugging without thinking about it.

Currently in `src/network.rs` (and analogous saorsa-gossip paths):
```rust
info!("[{}] recv: {} bytes ({:?}) from peer PeerId([{}...])", ...);
info!("[{}] send: {} bytes ({:?}) to peer {}", ...);
```

These fire on **every inbound/outbound gossip message** — orders of magnitude higher volume than warn-level events. At info-level on prod they generated 6-63 GB/day of syslog (see the 2026-05-16 sfo disk-full incident).

## Change

For each per-peer per-message event in `src/network.rs` and any analogous saorsa-gossip paths, change `info!` → `trace!`. Surface those events only when explicitly debugging with `RUST_LOG=trace`.

Candidates (the audit's hot offenders):
- `[N/M network] recv: ... bytes (StreamType) from peer PeerId(...)` 
- `[N/M network] send: ... bytes (StreamType) to peer PeerId(...)`
- Per-connection lifecycle logs that fire on every connection event

## Acceptance

- [ ] All per-peer per-message logs in src/network.rs at `info!` → `trace!`
- [ ] Equivalent in saorsa-gossip transport / pubsub if any exist
- [ ] Companion test: at `RUST_LOG=info` on a x0xd under sustained gossip load, journal volume stays below 1 M

issues.body:
## Context

Downstream (`saorsa-gossip`) builds the ant-quic `Node` via the simpler `NodeConfig::builder()` API. Today this builder does not expose a `max_message_size` knob — only the lower-level `P2pConfigBuilder` does.

Result: any consumer using `NodeConfigBuilder` is silently capped at the default 4 MiB per uni-stream send. Sending 10 MiB through `Node::send` triggers \`Connection closed: ReaderExit\` on the receiver and a send error on the sender, with no obvious surface to raise the cap.

issues.title: Proposal: POST /agent/sign — detached ML-DSA-65 signatures
issues.body:
x0xd already signs gossip frames at the transport layer, but transport-layer signatures don't survive a database read. Applications persisting signed records to disk or distributed storage (audit logs, governance votes, content provenance — anything with a future verifier who wasn't on the network when the signature was issued) need a way to produce a detached signature over arbitrary bytes using the same agent identity.

Today the only signing surfaces x0xd exposes are protocol-bound: `saorsa-gossip-identity` signs gossip frames automatically, and the named-groups `/groups/secure/open-envelope` is an ML-KEM-768 + AEAD opener, not a general-purpose signer. There's no "sign these bytes as me" primitive, even though the agent's secret key is right there.

## Proposed endpoint

```
POST /agent/sign
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{ "payload_b64": "<base64>" }
```

Returns:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "agent_id": "<hex, 64 chars>",
  "public_key_b64": "<base64>",
  "signature_b64": "<base64>",
  "algorithm": "ML-DSA-65"
}
```

256 KiB payload cap, bearer-token authenticated, rejects empty/malformed payloads, secret key never exposed. Caller picks the canonical serialization; x0xd doesn't interpret the bytes.

## Implementation available

Complete implementation on a fork branch (currently based on `main` at 3021cc5; I'll rebase forward onto 0.19.42 next):

issues.title: Replace fixed per-address direct-connect timeouts in P2pEndpoint with strategy-owned budgets
issues.body:
## Summary
`connect_with_fallback()` now derives adaptive direct / hole-punch / relay budgets from authoritative timeout owners plus RTT hints, but older direct-connect helpers in `P2pEndpoint` still contain fixed per-address dial timers.

## Remaining problem
Notable remaining examples:
- `try_connect_family(...)` still wraps each `connect_direct_addr()` in a fixed `5s` timeout
- `connect_dual_stack(...)` therefore still inherits a per-family fixed dial timeout path outside the newer adaptive strategy path

These helpers are now the main remaining direct-connect timeout assumptions in the P2P endpoint surface.

## Goal
Unify direct dialing around strategy-owned or caller-owned budgets so the endpoint no longer has split behavior between adaptive and fixed direct connection paths.

## Suggested slice
1. Audit all direct-dial entry points that bypass `connect_with_fallback()`
2. Thread explicit budgets or derive them from the same adaptive strategy logic
3. Add regression coverage for slow-but-live direct dial paths

## Acceptance criteria
- no production direct-connect helper relies on a fixed `5s` per-address timeout unless explicitly caller-owned
- dual-stack and fallback paths share the same timeout ownership model
- tests cover slower-path direct dialing without false failure

issues.title: Replace fixed NAT traversal phase durations with contract-driven budgets
issues.body:
## Summary
The recent timeout cleanup removed sleep-loop polling, discovery interval polling, legacy session polling ticks, and the `send().stopped()` false-liveness bug. The main remaining timeout debt inside NAT traversal is the set of fixed phase durations in `NatTraversalEndpoint::get_phase_timeout(...)` (for example discovery/synchronization/punching/connected stage defaults).

## Remaining problem
These phase durations still act like coarse truth about how long progress *should* take, even though the rest of the stack is moving toward:
- event-driven progression
- explicit caller-owned budgets
- timers only enforcing contracts about absence

Current examples include fixed fallback durations for:
- discovery
- synchronization
- punching
- connected keepalive/state checks

## Goal
Replace fixed phase durations with contract-driven budgeting that is informed by:
- configured coordination / connection-establishment timeouts
- observed RTT / coordinator quality when available
- explicit ownership of keepalive vs liveness vs orchestration deadlines

## Suggested slice
1. Audit all `get_phase_timeout(...)` consumers
2. Split phase deadlines into:
   - protocol contract deadlines
   - caller-owned orchestration budgets
   - maintenance / lease timers
3. Remove any stage timeouts that only exist as legacy polling fallbacks
4. Add regression coverage for slow-but-live paths so lower-latency assumptions cannot regress correctness

- no phase timeout is treat

issues.title: Consolidate timeout ownership and retire duplicate src/config/timeouts.rs
issues.body:
## Summary
`src/config/timeouts.rs` still exists as a duplicate/shadow timeout catalogue alongside the authoritative `src/config/nat_timeouts.rs` + transport defaults. Recent timeout-cleanup work moved more runtime behavior onto explicit owners (transport keepalive, NAT coordination timeout, adaptive connection strategy budgets), but this legacy module still invites drift and accidental reuse of stale constants.

issues.body:
## Summary

On the x0x VPS bootstrap fleet (5 nodes across NYC, SFO, Helsinki, Nuremberg, Tokyo on ant-quic 0.27.1), `node.send()` to a subset of currently-connected peers returns an error from the QUIC connection layer:

issues.title: C — DM ACK protocol and retry/receipt semantics
issues.body:
Fourth tranche of C. Binds sender-side send_direct to explicit receipt.

**Design doc**: [docs/design/dm-over-gossip.md](https://github.com/saorsa-labs/x0x/blob/claude/design-c-dm-over-gossip/docs/design/dm-over-gossip.md) (branch: \`claude/design-c-dm-over-gossip\`)

## Scope

### Sender
\`\`\`rust
pub async fn send_direct(&self, to: &AgentId, payload: Vec<u8>)
    -> Result<DmReceipt, DmError>;

pub struct DmReceipt {
    pub request_id: [u8; 16],
    pub accepted_at: Instant,
    pub retries_used: u8,
    pub path: DmPath,  // GossipInbox | RawQuic
}
\`\`\`

Happy path: publish \`Payload\` → await matching \`Ack\` on own inbox topic → resolve with \`DmReceipt\`. Default timeout 10 s per attempt.

Retry path: reuse the same \`request_id\` up to 3 times with exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s). Recipient's dedupe ensures no duplicate delivery; recipient re-ACKs with cached outcome. Sender stops on first valid ACK.

After the signature-first pipeline completes (envelope issue), receiver:
1. Delivers payload to local DM handler (broadcast channel to SSE / WS subscribers).
2. Emits \`Ack { acks_request_id, outcome: Accepted }\` on sender's inbox topic.

\`Ok(DmReceipt)\` means **recipient agent accepted the envelope into its DM handler**. It does NOT mean durable storage, UI display, or user read. This is the only receipt level v1 imple

issues.title: C — dedupe and replay protection for DM envelopes
issues.body:
Third tranche of C. Correctness gate — must land with the envelope work.

**Design doc**: [docs/design/dm-over-gossip.md](https://github.com/saorsa-labs/x0x/blob/claude/design-c-dm-over-gossip/docs/design/dm-over-gossip.md) (branch: \`claude/design-c-dm-over-gossip\`)

## Scope

- Dedupe key: \`(sender_agent_id, request_id: [u8; 16])\`.
- \`RecentDeliveryCache\` — LRU with 5-minute TTL, 10 000-entry max.
- Timestamp-acceptance window on receive:
  1. \`now >= created_at - 30s\` (backward skew tolerance)
  2. \`now < expires_at_unix_ms\`
  3. \`expires_at_unix_ms <= created_at + 10 min\` (cap envelope lifetime)
- Duplicate envelope handling:
  - First delivery: full processing path.
  - Subsequent deliveries of same \`(sender, request_id)\`: skip handler, re-ACK with cached outcome.
- Cached outcomes: \`Accepted\` or \`RejectedByPolicy { reason }\`.

## Acceptance

- Unit tests: TTL expiry, LRU eviction under pressure, timestamp edges (all 4).
- Integration: A sends same envelope twice → B delivers once, ACKs twice.
- Integration: envelope from "future" (created_at 2 min ahead) dropped.
- Integration: envelope past \`expires_at\` dropped.

Part of the x0x 0.18.0 milestone.
